hops.title: The pale-coat wiring of Siamese cats and white tigers
hops.text: Siamese cats are often cross-eyed, and white tigers sometimes are. In Siamese cats, the reduced pigment that pales the coat comes with unusual visual wiring: some fibers from the temple side of each retina cross to the wrong side of the brain and reach LGN layers meant for the other eye. In 1971 Hubel and Wiesel found no cells driven by both eyes in the cortex serving the cats' peripheral vision. One Siamese raised with both eyes closed did have them, suggesting the squint caused the loss. In 1973 Ray Guillery and Jon Kaas found a similar albinism-type abnormality in one white tiger's brain.

sources.citation: Hubel DH & Wiesel TN, J. Physiol. 218(1):33-62 (1971), PMID 5130620
Guillery RW & Kaas JH, Science 180(4092):1287-1289 (1973), PMID 4707916

image.caption: Siamese cats have unusual pale-coat visual wiring; one white tiger with aligned eyes showed a similar abnormality.

hops.title: After a patch, an adult's covered eye briefly wins
hops.text: Six days with one eye closed, at the peak of a kitten's window, leaves few cortical cells that eye can still drive. So it is tempting to assume an adult's patched eye loses ground too, only more slowly. In 2013, Claudia Lunghi, David Burr and Maria Concetta Morrone patched one eye of healthy adults for 150 minutes, then showed each eye a different striped pattern. With grayscale stripes, the patched eye's pattern stayed visible longer on average during the first 15 minutes. With brightness-matched color stripes, that effect still held 180 minutes later. The authors read it as homeostatic compensation: the adult system briefly turned up the deprived eye.

sources.citation: Lunghi C, Burr DC & Morrone MC, J. Vis. 13(6):1 (2013), PMID 23637272

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student removing a translucent eye patch beside shutter goggles and a screen showing two differently tilted striped patterns.
image.caption: After 150 minutes under a patch, an adult's covered eye briefly wins more of the contest between the eyes.

hops.title: The neurobiologist who gained stereo vision as an adult
hops.text: For years, Mount Holyoke College neurobiologist Susan Barry taught students that the brain is highly malleable in infancy but loses the capacity to rewire in adulthood. Cross-eyed since early infancy, she learned to shut down one eye's input to avoid double vision, and she grew up without stereo vision, the depth the brain computes by comparing the two eyes' images. In 2002 she began optometric vision therapy to train both eyes to aim at the same point. Buildings on street corners started to loom toward her like the bows of giant ships, and tree branches reached out into space. She began teaching adult plasticity differently.

sources.citation: Susan Barry faculty profile, Mount Holyoke College

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An autumn college street corner with a brick building and deeply layered tree branches behind an open notebook on a bench.
image.caption: After growing up without stereo vision, Susan Barry gained it as an adult through vision therapy.

audio.title: Cataracts, silent retinas and two-eyed Tetris
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories in which the contest between the two eyes leaves the textbook and turns up in clinics and labs.

The first comes from the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto. In nineteen ninety-five, Terri Lewis, Daphne Maurer and Henry Brent published a study of children born with dense cataracts. Sixty-three had a cloudy lens in one eye, and seventy-seven had cataracts in both. If plain disuse were the whole problem, two clouded eyes should be at least as hard to recover from as one. The data ran the other way. At twelve months and again at thirty to thirty-six months, children with one cataract whose clear eye had been patched for fewer than three hours a day, on average, did significantly worse with their treated eye on a test of how fine a set of stripes they could see than children treated at a comparable age for cataracts in both eyes. Children whose clear eye was patched at least three hours a day scored about the same as the two-cataract group. This was an observational study, not a trial, but the pattern suggests that competition from the clear eye added to the harm of early deprivation.

The second story takes the idea that silence is not the same as noise and pushes it further. One proposal is that a stretch of quiet makes synapses easier to strengthen later. In two thousand sixteen, Ming-fai Fong, Donald Mitchell, Kevin Duffy and Mark Bear, working at M I T and Dalhousie University, tested a prediction from that idea in two species. Suppose an eye has already lost cortical ground after early closure. What happens if you temporarily silence both retinas with a local anesthetic, let the drug wear off, and then give the animal ordinary two-eyed vision? In young mice, the lost cortical responses came back. In three-month-old kittens, past the peak of their window, a severe loss of acuity fully reversed. First both eyes went quiet. Then two-eyed vision gave the deprived eye its chance to recover.

The third story is about adults with amblyopia, well past the age at which patching is usually tried. Classic patching makes the weak eye work alone, but whenever both eyes are open, the stronger eye often keeps suppressing the weaker one. So in two thousand twelve and two thousand thirteen, Robert Hess and colleagues at McGill University and the University of Auckland adapted the falling-block game Tetris for virtual reality goggles and an iPod touch. The weaker eye saw blocks at full contrast. The stronger eye saw game elements at lower contrast, so they stood out less against the background, and players had to combine what both eyes saw to play at all. In small early studies, adults who trained this way showed weaker suppression and some gains in sharpness and depth perception. In an eighteen-person study from the same group, the two-eye training produced larger gains in sharpness and depth perception, and a larger drop in suppression, than making the weak eye work alone. The clinic has been a harder test. In two thousand eighteen, a randomized, double-masked trial that included some of the earlier researchers assigned a hundred and fifteen people, seven and older, to six weeks at home with either the two-eye game or a placebo version that showed both eyes the same images, and the two-eye game did no better on the vision tests. Getting the two eyes to cooperate helped in the lab; making it a reliable treatment is still unfinished work.
